name: AnyTool: Self-Reflective, Hierarchical Agents for Large-Scale API Calls
venue: ICML 2024 (also arXiv:2402.04253, submitted Feb 2024; DBLP: conf/icml/DuW024)
authors_affiliation: Yu Du (Tsinghua University); Fangyun Wei (Microsoft Research Asia, equal contribution); Hongyang Zhang (University of Waterloo, corresponding author).
maintained_repo_url: https://github.com/dyabel/AnyTool (single-contributor repo; last pushed 2024-03-26, not a continuously-maintained leaderboard) [uncertain]
task_domain: Tool-use: LLM-agent tool/API retrieval and invocation to answer user queries over a large-scale (16k+) real-world API pool (RapidAPI).
problem_setting: Interactive, training-free (plug-and-play) tool-use. Given a user query and a pool of 16,000+ RapidAPI APIs, an agent must (1) retrieve a small relevant API-candidate set from the full pool and (2) solve the query by calling those APIs. The system is a multi-agent hierarchy (meta-agent -> category agents -> tool agents) plus a single solver agent, all driven by GPT-4 function calling with no external module training. Operates under the assumption that some subset of APIs can resolve the query; supervision is limited to GPT-4 self-evaluation of solvability/solved (96.5% alignment with human evaluators).
what_is_retrieved: Tools / APIs (RapidAPI tool-API documents): the hierarchical retriever selects a set of relevant API candidates from the 16k+ pool, organized as category -> tool -> API.
retrieval_grounding: STATIC external corpus: the 16k+ RapidAPI API pool (as collected by ToolLLM/ToolBench) and its RapidAPI category->tool->API taxonomy. No growing/episodic memory persists across queries; the per-query API-candidate pool and agent histories are transient within a single query's reflection loop.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Completeness-oriented (recovery of the minimal needed set), NOT fixed top-k ranking: the retriever grows a variable-size API-candidate pool until a tool agent's 'check_if_request_solvable' returns True or a max-pool-size cap (default 64) is reached; self-reflection then re-expands the pool until the query is solved, aiming to recover the complete set of APIs needed (often multiple APIs across 2-5 categories).
cbr_cycle_coverage: Not framed as CBR. If forced to map: [Retrieve: partial - retrieves APIs not prior cases; Reuse: no; Revise: yes via self-reflection re-activation; Retain: no - nothing persisted across queries]. N/A as a CBR work.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it frames itself as a self-reflective hierarchical tool-retrieval agent.
retrieval_unit: tool-API (individual RapidAPI API endpoint, defined by category_name/tool_name/api_name plus its documentation: purpose, required/optional parameters, output types). The hierarchy also exposes coarser units: categories (tier 1) and tools (tier 2), but the retrieved/added candidates are individual APIs.
index_source: Static corpus, offline-defined: the 16k+ RapidAPI API pool from ToolLLM/ToolBench plus its fixed RapidAPI category->tool->API taxonomy. Not online-induced; the store is frozen. (Preprocessing scripts extract api/category/tool details and a tool 'database' for the agents to query.)
index_structure_topology: Hierarchical (3-tier): category -> tool -> API, mirroring the RapidAPI taxonomy. Realized as a divide-and-conquer agent hierarchy: a meta-agent dynamically spawns category agents, which spawn tool agents (each managing up to K=5 tools by default); tool agents add individual APIs to a shared global API-candidate pool. No flat vector index for the retriever itself (baselines like ToolLLM's retriever and AutoGen-RAG use flat dense indices).
retriever_type: LLM-as-retriever (generative agentic retrieval): GPT-4 function-calling agents directly explore the taxonomy and select APIs, with NO trained dense/sparse retriever and no external embedding model. (Contrasts with ToolLLM's fine-tuned dense retriever and AutoGen-RAG's embedding-based retriever used as baselines.)
retriever_learning_signal: None (off-the-shelf): the retriever is not trained or fine-tuned. It relies entirely on GPT-4's pretrained function-calling/linguistic comprehension. The only feedback signal is the in-context self-reflection 'fail reason' fed back to agents (LM-feedback at inference time), not a learned retriever objective.
query_construction: Raw user query Q is passed (with a bootstrap prompt and the function list) to the meta-agent; each tier-agent reasons over Q against the categories/tools/APIs it can see. No explicit query decomposition or synthetic-query expansion; intent handling is implicit via GPT-4 reasoning. On self-reflection, the query context is augmented with the identified failure reason.
query_granularity: Task-level: retrieval is driven by the whole user query Q (one query at a time), not per-reasoning-step. The hierarchical decomposition is over the API space (category/tool/API), not over sub-queries; multiple agents process Q in parallel (multi-threaded).
when_to_retrieve: Iterative / active (reflection-triggered): an initial retrieval+solve pass, then the self-reflection mechanism re-activates the retriever-and-solver loop whenever the solver fails (avg 4.6 self-reflections per query). Within the retriever, agents iteratively explore and add APIs until a solvability check passes.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Agent-initiated / reflection-triggered failure signal: re-retrieval is triggered when (1) the solver issues 'Give Up', or (2) the solver returns 'Give Solution' but GPT-4's evaluator judges the query still unsolved. The concrete signal is the GPT-4-/solver-provided 'fail reason', which is injected into agents' histories to re-activate them. Initial retrieval termination is triggered by a tool agent's 'check_if_request_solvable'=True or the API-candidate pool reaching max size.
reranking: No explicit reranking stage. Selection is via agentic decisions (tool agents call add_API_into_API_pool); a solvability check gates termination rather than scoring/reranking a ranked list. Self-reflection in the solver instead prunes APIs deemed irrelevant from the candidate pool.
retrieved_context_refinement: Yes, via self-reflection pruning: when the solver gives up it must name the irrelevant/non-working APIs; these are removed from the expanded API-candidate pool and the history items invoking them are excluded from the solver's context before re-activation. Otherwise no compression/distillation; agents fetch on-demand tool descriptions and API details (progressive disclosure of documentation).
tool_document_engineering: Raw RapidAPI documentation, accessed on demand and progressively: agents call get_tool_descriptions and get_API_detail to fetch tool/API descriptions, parameters, and output specs only when needed. No synthetic-query augmentation, expanded summaries, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings (those are absent because there is no trained retriever). Preprocessing extracts API/category/tool details into a queryable database.
index_content_separation: Yes (progressive disclosure): a lightweight navigable index (category names -> tool names -> API names) is separated from heavy content (full tool descriptions and API details) which agents load on demand via get_tool_descriptions / get_API_detail. This keeps each agent's context within GPT-4's max context length.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Static tool index (frozen 16k+ RapidAPI pool from ToolBench); integration protocol is RapidAPI (real RapidAPI calls via ToolBench's StableToolBench-style RapidAPI keys / function-calling). No live CRUD auto-sync, no MCP.
tool_dependency_awareness: Limited/implicit: no explicit inter-tool dependency graph or dependency-aware reranking. The solver (DFSDT over GPT-4 function calling) handles multi-API composition and ordering at solve time, and AnyToolBench queries require composing APIs from 2-5 categories, but dependencies are not modeled in the retriever index. [uncertain]
how_retrieved_used: Prompt augmentation for tool invocation: the retrieved API-candidate pool is supplied (with a bootstrap prompt and a 'finish' function) to the solver agent, which calls the APIs via GPT-4 function calling using DFSDT (or CoT) to produce the final answer. Retrieved APIs are executable functions, not just text exemplars.
planning_integration: Retrieve-then-plan (dual-phase), wrapped in a closed reflection loop: (phase 1) hierarchical retriever produces an API-candidate pool; (phase 2) the solver plans/acts over those APIs with DFSDT (depth-first search-based decision tree, allowing backtracking) or CoT. On failure, self-reflection re-activates retriever then solver, expanding/pruning the candidate pool. Planning is at the level of API-call sequences within the solver, not a tree search over retrieval itself.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Per-tool-call within a rollout (solver phase) and per-reflection-round at the system level. Retrieval is decoupled from per-CoT-step reasoning: retrieval happens in a dedicated phase and is re-invoked per self-reflection round (avg 4.6 rounds) rather than woven into every reasoning step.
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (not a CBR/case-adaptation method). The closest analogue is execution-feedback-driven revision: the self-reflection loop revises the API-candidate pool and re-runs the solver using the GPT-4/solver failure reason.
retrieved_item_representation: Executable tool/API functions injected into the solver's function list (GPT-4 function-calling schema with name, parameters, output spec), plus their RapidAPI documentation as context. Not raw trajectories or distilled strategies.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Procedural tool / executable API (single RapidAPI endpoint). Retrieval operates at concrete tool-API granularity, navigated via a coarser-to-finer abstraction (category -> tool -> API).
noise_robustness_mechanism: Self-reflection / relevance evaluation: a GPT-4 solvability+solution evaluator (96.5% human alignment) gates outcomes; the solver must identify and the system removes irrelevant/non-working APIs from the candidate pool before re-activation, reducing distractor APIs. Hierarchical decomposition also narrows each agent's search scope to reduce irrelevant context. No retriever-aware training or distractor-aware SFT (no training at all).
memory_type: None (no persistent cross-query memory). Within a single query it maintains transient per-agent historical contexts and a global API-candidate pool; these are not retained across queries.
write_back: False: the system does not store new experiences/cases/skills into any persistent memory for reuse on future queries. (Within-query: it does append failure reasons and explored APIs into transient agent histories, but this is discarded after the query.)
online_growth: No: the retrievable store (16k+ API pool and taxonomy) is frozen and does not grow during deployment. Only the transient per-query API-candidate pool grows within a query.
write_back_trigger: Never (no persistent write-back). For the transient within-query expansion, the trigger is reflective: after self-critique/failure (solver 'Give Up' or GPT-4 judging the solution unsolved), the failure reason is written into agent histories and new APIs are added to the candidate pool. Nothing is written to a durable store.
failure_experience_usage: Failures are used corrective and within-query only: the failure reason and the names of irrelevant/non-working APIs drive pruning (remove bad APIs) and re-expansion (add unexplored categories/tools/APIs). Failure experiences are NOT stored for retrieval on future queries (no cross-query failure memory).
memory_evolution_update: N/A for persistent memory. Within-query candidate-pool dynamics: append (add new APIs on re-activation) plus forget/prune (remove APIs flagged irrelevant by the solver), with agent histories augmented by the failure reason. No durable entries are mutated.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No: retrieval/API-selection is NOT a learned/RL-optimized policy. It is performed by frozen GPT-4 function-calling agents (zero training of external modules), guided by prompts and in-context feedback rather than a trained selection policy.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: Within-query multi-agent sharing only: meta/category/tool agents share a single global API-candidate pool and pass failure reasons across the hierarchy during one query. There is no cross-query or cross-framework memory sharing; nothing persists for other queries or external frameworks.
benchmarks: ToolBench (filtered, six subsets: G1-Instruction, G1-Tool, G1-Category, G2-Instruction, G2-Category, G3-Instruction; filtered counts 115/132/142/107/98/38 after manual removal of non-solvable queries), original ToolBench (Table 9), and AnyToolBench (new benchmark introduced here, 400 GPT-4-synthesized solvable instances).
benchmark_family: tool (ToolBench / RapidAPI tool-use); AnyToolBench is a new tool-use benchmark in the same RapidAPI family.
baselines: ToolLLM (ToolLLaMA w/ DFSDT, with ToolLLM's trained API retriever or OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 retriever) and its variants (GPT-4 w/ DFSDT as solver; reference-API-only no-retriever); GPT-4 with reference APIs (w/ CoT and w/ DFSDT); GPT-4 with a Plain Agent retriever; GPT-4 with AutoGen-RAG retriever (text-embedding-ada-002 and all-mpnet-base-v2); GPT-3.5 with reference APIs (w/ CoT and w/ DFSDT).
key_metrics: Pass rate (PR). The paper uses a revised pass rate R = #(Solved) / (#(Solved) + #(Unsolved)) on filtered ToolBench (Eq. 2 / Fig. 4(b)), correcting ToolLLM's R = (#(Non-solvable)+#(Solved)) / (#(Non-solvable)+#(Solved)+#(Unsolved)) which inflates pass rate (random APIs yield 99.0%). GPT-4 is the evaluator (96.5% human alignment).
headline_result: On filtered ToolBench, AnyTool reaches 58.2% average pass rate vs ToolLLM 22.9% (ToolLLM's retriever + ToolLLaMA w/ DFSDT), i.e. +35.4% (abstract) / +32.6 over original ToolLLM and +19.3 over GPT-4-with-reference-APIs (text). On AnyToolBench, AnyTool 73.8% vs best ToolLLM variant 36.6% and GPT-4 plain-agent 14.0%.
ablations: Component ablation (Table 3, G2-I/G3-I): full AnyTool 58.9/63.2; -Hierarchical Structure (flat retriever) 22.4/15.8; -Self-Reflection 19.6/15.8; -DFSDT/+CoT 50.5/60.3 (drop of 8.4/2.9). Self-reflection re-activation scope (Table 4): tool agents only 43.9/44.7; +category agents 55.2/55.3; all agents 58.9/63.2. API pool size (Table 5): 1k=18.6/7.9, 5k=26.3/23.7, 10k=38.1/36.8, all=58.9/63.2 (larger pool helps). Max API-candidate pool size (Table 6): 16=49.5/42.1, 32=58.9/55.3, 64=58.9/63.2 (saturates ~64). Max tools per tool agent K (Table 7): K=3 -> 48.6/42.1, K=5 -> 58.9/57.9, K=10 -> 52.3/39.5 (trade-off, best K=5). Plain-agent info ablation (Table 10) and AutoGen-RAG embedding ablation (Table 11) show all near 13-16%, far below AnyTool.
evaluation_decoupling: No: the paper reports only end-to-end pass rate. It does NOT report intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / retrieval completeness) separately; retrieval quality is assessed indirectly through end-task pass rate and the API-pool/candidate-pool ablations.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Primarily outcome (pass rate). Some process-level statistics are reported (avg self-reflection rounds, avg agent quantity, avg API-candidate count, token/call counts), and a solvability-vs-solved decomposition exists, but there is no step-wise reasoning-faithfulness or trajectory-quality score.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Reported consumption (Table 12, avg over datasets): ~13.5-13.6 x 10^4 tokens per query, 14.1 API candidates, 43.3 OpenAI API calls, and 4.6 self-reflections per query. With only 4-6 self-reflection rounds pass rate improves by up to 20% across datasets. Wall-clock latency deemed infeasible to measure due to unstable GPT-4 server response. Self-reflection reduces 'over-search' on simple queries while enabling deeper search on complex ones.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Completeness-/saturation-driven variable-size selection, budget-capped: the API-candidate pool grows until a solvability check passes or a maximal pool size is reached (default max_api_number=64; performance saturates ~64, with 32 also strong). Hierarchy + progressive disclosure keep each agent within GPT-4's max context length; actual avg APIs used per query ~14.1.
benchmark_construction_and_size: AnyToolBench: 400 instances, LLM-synthesized by prompting GPT-4 to freely explore the API pool (get_tools_in_category/get_tool_descriptions/get_APIs_in_tool/get_API_detail), add real APIs via add_API_into_API_pool, synthesize parameters, and formulate queries from actual API responses (composing 2-5 categories), with GPT-4-generated reference solutions verified to truly resolve the query (ensuring solvability and reducing hallucination). Also constructs a filtered ToolBench via manual review removing non-solvable queries (115/132/142/107/98/38 per subset). Answers verified via GPT-4 evaluation (96.5% human alignment). Difficulty signal: best system (AnyTool) reaches 73.8% PR on AnyToolBench and 58.2% avg on filtered ToolBench.
builds_on: ToolLLM / ToolBench (Qin et al., 2023b; 16k+ RapidAPI pool, dual-phase retrieve-then-solve, DFSDT solver, ToolLLaMA) which AnyTool reuses and extends; GPT-4 function calling (Achiam et al., 2023); DFSDT and CoT (Wei et al., 2022); self-reflection literature in LLMs.
contrasts_with: ToolLLM's trained dense API retriever and ToolLLaMA solver; embedding-based retrieval (OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002, all-mpnet-base-v2 via AutoGen-RAG); flat GPT-4 plain-agent retrieval; and ToolLLM's evaluation protocol (which inflates pass rate by counting non-solvable queries as passes). AnyTool argues against trained retrievers (low accuracy, no feedback) in favor of training-free hierarchical GPT-4 retrieval with self-reflection.
lineage: Group E (tool-use). Lineage: large-scale real-world API tool-use after ToolLLM/ToolBench; pioneers training-free, LLM-as-retriever hierarchical (category/tool/API) retrieval with a self-reflective re-activation loop, and introduces AnyToolBench plus a corrected pass-rate evaluation protocol. A precursor to later tool-retrieval works emphasizing tool-document engineering, dependency-aware and MCP/live tool indices.
